stem: A jar contains 9 red candies, 5 yellow candies, and 3 green candies. If one candy is selected at random, what is the probability that it is yellow?
explanation: The total number of candies is 9 + 5 + 3 = 17. The probability of selecting a yellow candy is \frac{5}{17}. The value \frac{5}{14} incorrectly uses 9 + 5 = 14 as the total, omitting the green candies. The value \frac{5}{12} uses 9 + 3 = 12 as the total, omitting the yellow candies from the denominator while counting them in the numerator. The value \frac{3}{17} uses the count of green candies in the numerator instead of the count of yellow candies.

stem: A survey of 200 employees found that 87 drink coffee, 53 drink tea, and 19 drink both coffee and tea. If an employee is selected at random, what is the probability that the employee drinks coffee or tea?
explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle, P(coffee or tea) = P(coffee) + P(tea) - P(both) = \frac{87 + 53 - 19}{200} = \frac{121}{200}. The value \frac{140}{200} adds coffee and tea drinkers without subtracting those who drink both, double-counting the 19 overlap. The value \frac{87}{200} counts only coffee drinkers, ignoring tea drinkers entirely. The value \frac{159}{200} results from adding all three values (87 + 53 + 19) instead of subtracting the overlap.

stem: In a class of 150 students, 62 study French, 41 study German, and 23 study both French and German. If a student who studies French is selected at random, what is the probability that this student also studies German?
explanation: This is a conditional probability question: P(German | French) = \frac{P(\text{French and German})}{P(\text{French})} = \frac{23}{62}. The value \frac{23}{150} divides by the total number of students rather than the number of French students, computing an unconditional probability instead of a conditional one. The value \frac{23}{41} divides by the number of German students, computing P(French | German) instead of P(German | French) — reversing the conditioning event. The value \frac{23}{80} uses 62 + 41 - 23 = 80 (the union) as the denominator, confusing the size of the union with the size of the conditioning event.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 400 voters in a city found that 58% support a new park initiative. The margin of error for the survey is 4 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Between 54% and 62% of all voters in the city are likely to support the initiative.
Exactly 58% of all voters in the city support the initiative.
Between 54% and 62% of the surveyed voters changed their minds during the survey.
The survey is inaccurate because the margin of error is too large.

explanation: A margin of error of 4 percentage points means the plausible range for the true population proportion is 58% minus 4% to 58% plus 4%, or 54% to 62%. Claiming exactly 58% ignores the inherent uncertainty of sampling — the margin of error exists precisely because a sample statistic is an estimate, not an exact value. The interpretation about surveyed voters changing their minds confuses margin of error with response variability. Declaring the survey inaccurate based solely on having a margin of error misunderstands the concept; all surveys have margins of error, and 4 points is within a normal range for this sample size.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Two independent random samples are taken from the same population. Sample A has 250 respondents and finds that 47% prefer Brand X, with a margin of error of 6.2 percentage points. Sample B has 1,000 respondents and finds that 43% prefer Brand X, with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points. Which of the following statements is best supported by these results?

options.text: Sample A is more reliable because it shows a higher preference for Brand X.
The confidence intervals from the two samples overlap, so the results are consistent with each other.
Sample B proves that exactly 43% of the population prefers Brand X.
The two samples contradict each other, so at least one must have a biased methodology.

explanation: Sample A's confidence interval is 40.8% to 53.2%, and Sample B's confidence interval is 39.9% to 46.1%. These intervals overlap substantially, meaning the two results are consistent with each other and could reflect the same true population parameter. A higher point estimate does not make a sample more reliable — reliability depends on sample size and methodology, not the magnitude of the result. No sample proves an exact population value; a sample statistic is always an estimate with uncertainty. Two samples yielding different point estimates is expected due to sampling variability; overlapping confidence intervals indicate the difference is within normal variation, not evidence of bias.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 625 households and finds that 312 have at least one pet. Using the formula for the margin of error at a 95% confidence level, \text{margin of error} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, what is the approximate margin of error for this survey, expressed as a percent? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
explanation: The formula gives margin of error \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{625}} = \frac{1}{25} = 0.04, which is 4%. The sample proportion (312 out of 625 = 49.92%) is not needed to apply this simplified margin of error formula — the formula depends only on the sample size n. A common error is to use the number of households with pets (312) instead of the total sample size (625) in the denominator, which would give \frac{1}{\sqrt{312}} \approx 0.0566 or about 6%. Another error is forgetting to convert the decimal 0.04 to a percentage, giving 0.04 instead of 4.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A health magazine reports that people who eat breakfast every day have lower rates of heart disease than people who skip breakfast. The magazine concludes that eating breakfast prevents heart disease. Which of the following is the most significant flaw in this conclusion?

options.text: The study did not include enough participants.
The study is observational and cannot establish that eating breakfast causes lower heart disease rates.
The magazine should have studied lunch habits instead of breakfast habits.
People who eat breakfast always have healthier diets overall.

explanation: The study described is observational — it compares outcomes between groups that naturally differ in behavior. Observational studies can identify associations but cannot establish causation because confounding variables (such as overall lifestyle, exercise habits, or socioeconomic status) may explain the difference. Citing insufficient participants is not identified as a problem in the scenario and does not address the core logical flaw. Suggesting lunch should be studied instead is irrelevant to the causal reasoning error. Asserting that breakfast eaters always have healthier diets overall is an unsupported generalization that itself commits the same correlation-causation error.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A pharmaceutical company tested a new allergy medication. They recruited 300 volunteers who suffer from seasonal allergies and randomly assigned 150 to receive the medication and 150 to receive a placebo. After 6 weeks, the medication group reported 37% fewer allergy symptoms than the placebo group. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this study design?

options.text: The medication causes a reduction in allergy symptoms compared to the placebo.
The medication would work equally well for people without seasonal allergies.
Allergy symptoms naturally decrease over any 6-week period.
Volunteers who chose the medication group had milder allergies to begin with.

explanation: Because the study used random assignment to divide participants into treatment and control groups, it is a randomized controlled experiment. This design controls for confounding variables and supports a causal conclusion: the medication caused the observed reduction in symptoms. Generalizing the result to people without seasonal allergies goes beyond the study population — the conclusion applies only to the population from which the sample was drawn. Claiming symptoms naturally decrease ignores the comparison with the placebo group, which controls for natural changes over time. Stating that participants chose the medication group contradicts the study design, which specifies random assignment, not self-selection.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A university researcher wants to determine whether a new tutoring method improves exam scores. She selects 80 students from a large introductory biology course and randomly assigns 40 to the new tutoring method and 40 to the traditional tutoring method. At the end of the semester, students using the new method scored an average of 7 points higher on the final exam. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The new tutoring method causes higher exam scores for all college students.
The new tutoring method causes higher exam scores for students similar to those in the introductory biology course.
There is an association, but not necessarily a causal relationship, between the new tutoring method and higher exam scores.
The study is invalid because the researcher should have used students from multiple courses.

explanation: Because the study uses random assignment, it can establish a causal relationship between the tutoring method and exam scores. However, the participants were drawn from one introductory biology course, so the causal conclusion can be generalized only to students similar to those in that course — not to all college students. Claiming the result applies to all college students overgeneralizes beyond the study population. Describing the finding as merely an association underestimates the strength of the conclusion available from a randomized experiment — random assignment specifically enables causal inference. Declaring the study invalid because it used only one course confuses generalizability with validity; the study is internally valid due to random assignment, even though its external generalizability is limited.
